analysis.one_liner: Raises fuel economy standards for all cars and light trucks four percent per year, with new tax credits for efficient vehicles.
analysis.headline: With 10 cosponsors from both parties, the bill never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required cars, SUVs, and pickups to get more miles per gallon — a four percent improvement each year, starting with passenger cars in model year 2009 and extending the same rules to every vehicle under 10,000 pounds starting in model year 2012. It also removed the limit on the tax credit buyers get for purchasing hybrids, extended that credit, and created a new tax credit covering 35 percent of the cost of retooling U.S. factories to build advanced-technology vehicles. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save money at the pump as new vehicles became more efficient; taxpayers and national security hawks, since the bill's stated aim was cutting the roughly 60 percent of U.S. oil that was imported at the time; and autoworkers and hybrid manufacturers, who would benefit from the new production tax credit and uncapped consumer credits.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the passenger car fuel economy standard to rise four percent per year for model years 2009 through 2011, on top of the existing minimums.

Sets an average standard of 27.5 miles per gallon for all automobiles by model year 2012, rising four percent per year thereafter, and extends fuel economy rules to all vehicles up to 10,000 pounds — closing the gap that had let many SUVs and light trucks be held to weaker standards than cars.

Removes the cap on the number of hybrid and advanced lean-burn vehicles eligible for the consumer tax credit and extends the credit through 2010, lowering the effective price of efficient vehicles for buyers.

Creates a tax credit worth 35 percent of the cost of retooling or expanding U.S. factories to build hybrid, electric, and other advanced-technology vehicles, which the bill's findings say could add roughly 60,000 domestic jobs.
Allows manufacturers to trade fuel-economy credits with each other and to spread compliance over up to four model years, giving them flexible ways to meet the higher standards.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of engineering more efficient fleets, with much of that cost likely passed to new-car buyers in higher prices; and the federal treasury, which would forgo revenue from the expanded consumer credits and the new manufacturing credit. Oil sellers would also lose sales as demand for gasoline declined.

drawbacks.text: Tighter standards raise manufacturing costs, and the bill's own findings note industry studies projecting billions in lost profits and hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk if fuel prices rose without efficiency gains — though the bill argued efficiency mandates were the answer rather than the problem.

The bill includes a broad escape valve: the Transportation Secretary may set lower standards if they are judged technologically unachievable, materially unsafe, or not cost-effective, which could let future administrations weaken the mandate.
A manufacturer's fleet can sit as much as 8 percent below the projected industry-wide average under the bill's 92 percent floor, softening how hard the mandate binds on any individual company.

Safety was the standard objection to higher fuel economy, on the theory that meeting standards means building lighter cars; the bill's text counters this with National Academies and independent studies finding efficiency and safety can improve together, but the concern was the core of the industry's argument against such bills.

The tax credits are real federal revenue losses, and the manufacturing credit is open to any taxpayer deriving more than 20 percent of gross receipts from vehicle manufacturing, a broad eligibility rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: buyers pay somewhat more for new vehicles but recoup it in fuel savings over the life of the car, while the country imports less oil. The design is reasonably careful — flexibility through credit trading and multi-year compliance, and credits to help factories convert — but the cost-effectiveness escape valve and the 92 percent floor give the industry room to dilute the mandate, and the manufacturing credits are a real cost to taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never considered it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Barack Obama introduced the bill on July 19, 2006, joined on introduction by seven other senators including Republicans Richard Lugar and Gordon Smith.
Ten senators cosponsored the bill in total: six Democrats and four Republicans.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction.
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a committee markup or a floor vote.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers that preferred the existing lighter standards were better off, since no higher mandate was ever imposed; gasoline sellers also kept a status quo in which demand for their product was untouched. Drivers gained nothing, continuing to face stagnant fuel economy and high gas prices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was genuinely bipartisan — of its 10 cosponsors, 6 were Democrats and 4 were Republicans — but it died without a vote in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: Higher standards would have forced costly re-engineering of their fleets, but the bill also handed them a 35 percent tax credit for retooling plants to build hybrids and electric vehicles, plus uncapped consumer credits that would boost sales of those models. Their interest in avoiding the mandate ran against drivers' interest in fuel savings, which is why they fought such bills.

The bill's whole premise was cutting gasoline demand — the bill's findings say passenger vehicles account for over 60 percent of transportation oil use. More efficient cars would mean less fuel sold, and any such loss for the industry was a saving for drivers.

industries.industry: Hybrid, electric, and battery component makers
industries.note: Removing the cap on the consumer hybrid credit and creating the manufacturing investment credit directly subsidizes the market for advanced-technology vehicles and the factories that build them. Cheaper efficient cars benefit buyers at the same time.
